text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, facing a crumbling peace process with the PLO, has said he is considering forming a "national unity" government with the main opposition Labour party.
Netanyahu confirmed what had been rumoured for weeks during several weekend interviews with Israeli reporters in Italy where he is on an official visit.
"I am already thinking about it...but I haven't reached a conclusion," said Netanyahu when asked if he would consider forming a unity government.
"I have consulted with friends, with several ministers in the government...Some have clear answers, some are wavering like I am on this matter," he told Israel Television on Friday.

Israeli-Palestinian peace moves came to a halt nearly a month ago when Netanyahu sent bulldozers to break ground on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem which Palestinians say violates peace agreements and international law.

Since then Israeli airwaves have buzzed with reports of contacts between Netanyahu's Likud party and the left-centre Labour party which led Israel to a breakthrough 1993 interim accord with the PLO and subsequent peace deals.

The right-wing Netanyahu, elected last May, opposed the agreements with the PLO but has promised to honour them. His religious and ultra-nationalist coalition partners accuse him of ceding too much to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
An Israeli decision last month to pull troops out of nine percent of the West Bank barely passed in Netanyahu's cabinet. Arafat refused the offer, saying he had expected three times as much land.
Settlement construction in East Jerusalem has sparked daily clashes between Palestinians and Israeli troops in the West Bank.
Dozens of Palestinian stone-throwers battled Israeli troops on Saturday in the West Bank town of Hebron where much of the unrest has been centred.

"If we are approached (about forming a national unity government), we will discuss it," said Labour party leader Shimon Peres, who helped engineer the PLO peace deals but lost last year's election to Netanyahu.
Peres, a Nobel peace prize laureate, has said a unity government is the only way to save peace moves with the PLO and other Arab partners.
But he has formally postponed the issue until a criminal investigation against members of Netanyahu's cabinet is cleared up. Police have said the investigation will last several more weeks.
Netanyahu has proposed defusing the crisis with the Palestinians by skipping interim steps and launching intensive negotiations culminating in a final peace agreement within six to nine months.
"I am considering one fundamental question...will expanding the government bring about a better result in our ability to conduct these negotiations (with the PLO) and complete them," said Netanyahu.

Israel and the PLO have left the most sensitive issues in their conflict to "final status" talks, including the permanent status of the West Bank and Gaza, the fate of Jerusalem and the future of Jewish settlments. Palestinians are suspicious that moving directly to these issues could mean Israel reneging on agreed interim steps.
